text:
I need to make a painful confession: somehow, LinkedIn has become an important social network to me. This isnât necessarily due to LinkedInâs sparkling competence, of course. To the contrary, LinkedIn is the Gerald Ford of social networks: the normal one that was left standing as the Richard Nixons and the Spiro Agnews of social media imploded around them. As with Gerald Ford, with LinkedIn we know that weâre getting something a bit clumsy and boring, but (as with post-Watergate America!), weâre also getting something that isnât totally crookedâââand thatâs actually a bit of a relief.
But because I am finding I am spending more time here, we need to have some real talk: too many of you are using LLMs to generate content. Now, this isnât entirely your fault: as if LLMs werenât tempting enough, LinkedIn itself is cheerfully (insistently!) offering to help you "rewrite it with AI." It seems so excited to help you out, why not let it chip in and ease your own burden?
Because holy hell, the writing sucks. Itâs not that itâs mediocre (though certainly that!), itâs that it is so stylistically grating, riddled with emojis and single-sentence paragraphs and "itâs not justâ¦â but also" constructions and (yes!) em-dashes that some of us use naturallyâââbut most donât (or shouldnât).
When you use an LLM to author a post, you may think you are generating plausible writing, but you arenât: to anyone who has seen even a modicum of LLM-generated content (a rapidly expanding demographic!), the LLM tells are impossible to ignore. Bluntly, your intellectual fly is open: lots of people noticeâââbut no one is pointing it out. And the problem isnât merely embarrassment: when youâââperson whose perspective I want to hear!âââare obviously using an LLM to write posts for you, I donât know whatâs real and what is in fact generated fanfic. You definitely donât sound like you, soâ¦â is the actual content real? I mean, maybe? But also maybe not. Regardless, I stop readingâââand so do lots of others.
To be clear, I think LLMs are incredibly useful: they are helpful for brainstorming, invaluable for comprehending text, and they make for astonishingly good editors. (And, unlike most good editors, you can freely ignore their well-meaning suggestions without fear of igniting a civil war over the Oxford comma or whatever.) But LLMs are also lousy writers and (most importantly!) they are not you. At best, they will wrap your otherwise real content in constructs that cause people to skim or otherwise stop reading; at worst, they will cause people who see it for what it is to question your authenticity entirely.
So please, if not for the sanity of all of us than just to give your own message the credit it deserves: have some confidence in your own voiceâââand write your own content.
